title: Yeast nutrients (YAN)
what: Whether to top up the must's yeast-assimilable nitrogen (YAN) with diammonium phosphate (DAP) before fermentation, or leave it as it is.

steps: also cuts the yeast's ester production
so the wine is less fruity as well as at risk of reduction

choose: Measure, then decide: below about 140–150 mg/L, add DAP. Adding by default is no free insurance: excess nitrogen drives a hotter ferment with more volatile acidity and microbial instability. If H₂S appears, aerate early; copper fining removes what persists. Intermediate YAN gives the best balance.
exam: Questions ask why nutrients are added or how a fault arises. Explain low nitrogen → stressed yeast → H₂S → a reduced, rotten-egg smell, and name the remedy.

check.question: A must at 22 °Brix has YAN 95 mg/L, and the cellar skips nutrients. What is the most likely result?
options: A sluggish fermentation and a rotten-egg (H₂S) smell
Extra fruity esters from slower yeast
A clean wine: yeast only run short above 25 °Brix
A faster fermentation that finishes early
check.answer: A sluggish fermentation and a rotten-egg (H₂S) smell
check.why: 95 mg/L is far below the roughly 140 mg/L threshold. Nitrogen-starved yeast ferment slowly, release H₂S and make fewer esters.

simplification: Game simplification: the nitrogen need rises 25 mg/L per °Brix above 20 (a heuristic), and the DAP option tops a must up only when it is short, so over-feeding is not modelled.
